note: Attacker-controlled text input includes a three-glyph sequence that exercises the morx state machine path for this font.

The morx contextual driver processes the glyph stream and can carry a marked glyph across state transitions; the current index and mark state determine whether substitutions are applied at end-of-text.
When a mark substitution succeeds, the code marks a range as unsafe to break using the saved mark index, propagating attacker-controlled shaping state into buffer metadata.
The unsafe-to-break helper scans the selected range and rewrites cluster metadata for the affected glyphs, so malformed state can influence later buffer operations.
Cluster and mask updates are applied in-place to the glyph info array, which is the propagation point from attacker-controlled shaping input to memory writes.

The current-glyph substitution path computes an index from buffer length; if the buffer is empty or state is inconsistent, this arithmetic is the root cause for an out-of-bounds access risk in the subsequent lookup and write path.

The glyph codepoint is read from the computed index and used to drive substitution lookup; this is the memory-safety sink because the code assumes the index is valid while operating on attacker-influenced buffer state.
